promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.

learningObjectives.title: Receptors are proteins that bind one specific ligand
Bacteria count themselves with a shared secreted signal
Four functional categories of animal signalling chemicals
Hormones act far away; neurotransmitters act next door
Surface receptors for ligands that stay out; internal receptors for ligands that get in
Neurotransmitter receptors open channels and change the voltage
Epinephrine acts through a G protein and cAMP
Insulin's receptor phosphorylates itself, and glucose transporters arrive
What oestradiol does in the hypothalamus and progesterone in the endometrium
Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it
A neuron is one cell with a body and long fibres
Pumping ions sets up the resting potential
Wider and myelinated fibres conduct faster
Synapses join neurons to neurons or to effectors, one way only
Neurotransmitter opens channels and depolarizes the postsynaptic cell
Local currents carry the action potential along
Reading an oscilloscope trace
Chemicals from outside can block or prolong transmission
Inhibitory neurotransmitters make the inside more negative
Free nerve endings detect painful stimuli; the brain feels pain

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a ligand and its receptor?
options: The ligand binds reversibly to a binding site on the receptor protein that is complementary to it, and the receptor changes shape.
The receptor's binding site converts the ligand into a product, in the way an enzyme's active site converts a substrate.
Any ligand reaching a cell binds to it, because every cell carries receptors for every signalling chemical in the body.
The ligand passes through a channel in the receptor into the cytoplasm, where it brings about the response directly.
optionWhy: A receptor is a protein with a binding site specific to its ligand. Binding is reversible and does not alter the ligand; the conformational change in the receptor is what initiates the cell's response.
A student who transfers the enzyme model to receptors picks this. A receptor does not catalyse a change in its ligand; the ligand dissociates unchanged and it is the receptor that changes shape.

A student who thinks arrival of a chemical is what causes a response picks this. Cells carry receptors only for particular ligands, so a signalling chemical acts only on cells with a complementary binding site.
A student who pictures the signalling chemical doing the job itself picks this. Binding to the receptor sets off a sequence of responses inside the cell; the ligand itself usually never enters.
questions.explain: A receptor is a protein with a binding site specific to its ligand. Binding is reversible and does not alter the ligand; the conformational change in the receptor is what initiates the cell's response.

questions.q: What is quorum sensing in bacteria?
options: Bacteria counting neighbouring cells through direct contact between the surface proteins of their cell walls.
Bacteria of one species each responding on their own to the concentration of nutrients in their environment.
Bacteria secreting a chemical that itself gives out light once enough of it has built up around the cells.
A change in gene expression across a population when a secreted signal reaches a threshold concentration.
optionWhy: A student who expects a head-count to need contact picks this. Density is sensed indirectly, through the concentration of a chemical that every cell secretes into the surroundings.
A student who thinks unicellular organisms do not signal to each other picks this. Quorum sensing is a response to a chemical made by the bacteria, coordinated across the population.

A student who thinks the signalling chemical performs the response picks this. The autoinducer is a ligand: it binds a receptor that promotes transcription of the lux genes, and the enzyme luciferase makes the light.

Each cell secretes an autoinducer; its concentration rises with population density, and above a threshold it binds receptors and alters gene expression in all the cells, as in bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri.
questions.explain: Each cell secretes an autoinducer; its concentration rises with population density, and above a threshold it binds receptors and alters gene expression in all the cells, as in bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri.

questions.q: Which statement about the functional categories of signalling chemicals in animals is correct?
options: Cytokines are small proteins, secreted mainly by cells of the immune system, that act mostly on nearby cells.
Calcium ions are secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood and carried to distant target organs.
Cytokines are secreted by endocrine glands into the blood, from which they act on distant organs.
Neurotransmitters are carried in the blood from a neuron to the target cells of distant organs.
optionWhy: Cytokines are produced by ordinary cells rather than endocrine glands and coordinate local responses, especially among immune cells; this local action distinguishes them from hormones.
A student who pictures calcium as a substance carried in blood picks this. Calcium ions signal within cells: a rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ when channels open triggers responses such as contraction.
A student who files every new chemical messenger as a hormone picks this. Cytokines come from cells such as immune cells, not glands, and act mainly locally.
A student who thinks all chemical messengers travel in blood picks this. A neurotransmitter diffuses across a synaptic gap of about 20 nm to the adjacent cell and acts locally.
questions.explain: Cytokines are produced by ordinary cells rather than endocrine glands and coordinate local responses, especially among immune cells; this local action distinguishes them from hormones.

questions.q: Chemical X is released from one cell, diffuses about 20 nm and acts on a single adjacent cell within a millisecond before being broken down. Chemical Y is released into the blood and, over several minutes, acts on cells in the liver, heart and skeletal muscle. Which statement is correct?
options: X is a neurotransmitter acting locally across a synaptic gap, and Y is a hormone acting at a distance after transport in the blood.
Both are hormones, because a chemical released from a cell to act on another cell has to travel through the blood.
Y is a neurotransmitter, because a hormone would be delivered by the blood to a single target organ rather than to several.
X acts faster because it enters the target cell and carries out the response itself, whereas Y has to bind a receptor.
optionWhy: The 20 nm diffusion distance, millisecond timing and single target cell are the marks of a neurotransmitter; transport in the blood and effects on cells in several organs over minutes are the marks of a hormone.
A student who thinks every chemical messenger uses the blood picks this. X crosses a synaptic gap by diffusion and never enters the blood.
A student who thinks the blood routes a hormone to a single organ picks this. The blood distributes a hormone everywhere, so acting on several organs is typical of a hormone, not evidence against it.

A student who pictures the signalling chemical doing the job itself picks this. X binds a receptor on the adjacent cell; its speed comes from the tiny distance it diffuses, not from entering the cell.
questions.explain: The 20 nm diffusion distance, millisecond timing and single target cell are the marks of a neurotransmitter; transport in the blood and effects on cells in several organs over minutes are the marks of a hormone.

questions.q: Insulin is a hydrophilic protein and oestradiol is a hydrophobic steroid. Where are their receptors, and do the hormones enter their target cells?
options: Both stay outside and bind receptors on the cell surface, because all receptors are proteins embedded in the plasma membrane.
Insulin stays outside and binds a transmembrane receptor; oestradiol passes through the membrane and binds an intracellular receptor.
Both enter the cell, because a signalling chemical has to reach the cytoplasm in order to bring about any response at all.
Insulin stays outside and binds a transmembrane receptor; oestradiol is carried through the membrane by a transport protein to a receptor inside.
optionWhy: A student who has only seen surface receptors picks this. Steroid hormones penetrate the cell and bind intracellular receptors, which then act on DNA.

A hydrophilic protein cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer, so its receptor spans the plasma membrane and the ligand remains outside. A hydrophobic steroid dissolves through the bilayer to reach a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
A student who believes hormones enter cells to act picks this. Insulin, being a hydrophilic protein, cannot cross the membrane; its signal is passed inside by the receptor.

A student who thinks hydrophobic molecules are excluded by the membrane picks this. Steroids dissolve through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer by simple diffusion; no carrier is needed to reach the intracellular receptor.
questions.explain: A hydrophilic protein cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer, so its receptor spans the plasma membrane and the ligand remains outside. A hydrophobic steroid dissolves through the bilayer to reach a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

questions.q: Acetylcholine released at a neuromuscular junction binds to acetylcholine receptors in the membrane of a muscle fibre. What happens next?
options: An ion channel in the receptor opens, positive ions diffuse into the fibre and the membrane potential becomes less negative.
Acetylcholine passes through the channel in the receptor, carrying its positive charge into the fibre with it.
An ion channel in the receptor opens, positively charged ions leave the fibre and the inside becomes more negative.
Acetylcholine enters the fibre and binds directly to the contractile proteins, causing them to shorten at once.
optionWhy: The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel. Binding opens the channel, Na+ diffuses in down its concentration gradient, and the resulting depolarization may trigger contraction.
A student who thinks the channel is for the ligand picks this. Acetylcholine stays bound on the outside; it is Na+ that diffuses through the opened channel.
A student who has the direction of ion movement or the sign convention reversed picks this. Na+ is concentrated outside, so it enters, and inflow of positive charge depolarizes the membrane.
A student who thinks the signalling chemical performs the response itself picks this. Contraction follows a change in membrane potential set off by the receptor; acetylcholine never enters the fibre.
questions.explain: The acetylcholine receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel. Binding opens the channel, Na+ diffuses in down its concentration gradient, and the resulting depolarization may trigger contraction.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events after epinephrine (adrenaline) binds to its receptor on a liver cell?
options: A G protein is activated, adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP, and cAMP activates kinases that switch on glycogen breakdown.
Epinephrine enters the liver cell and directly activates the enzymes that break down glycogen into glucose.
cAMP is released from the liver cell into the blood as a second messenger that acts on other liver cells.
The activated G protein converts ATP into cAMP, and the cAMP then breaks glycogen down directly into glucose.
optionWhy: The epinephrine receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor. The activated G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, the second messenger cAMP activates protein kinases, and the phosphorylated enzymes break down glycogen to release glucose.
A student who thinks hormones enter their target cells picks this. Epinephrine is hydrophilic and stays outside; the message is carried inside by the G protein and cAMP.
A student who reads 'second messenger' as a second hormone picks this. cAMP is made and acts within the cell; it is called a second messenger because it relays the hormone's message inside the cell.
A student who collapses the pathway picks this. Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, and cAMP acts by activating kinases; it does not hydrolyse glycogen itself.
questions.explain: The epinephrine receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor. The activated G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, the second messenger cAMP activates protein kinases, and the phosphorylated enzymes break down glycogen to release glucose.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes how insulin increases glucose uptake by a muscle cell?
options: Insulin enters the cell bound to glucose and releases it in the cytoplasm; the empty insulin then returns to the blood to collect more glucose.
Insulin binds the receptor, which phosphorylates free tyrosine in the cytoplasm; the phosphorylated tyrosine then binds glucose molecules and pulls them into the cell.
Insulin binds the receptor outside; tyrosines on its cytoplasmic part are phosphorylated; a cascade moves vesicles with glucose transporters to the membrane.
Insulin binds the receptor; the signal activates transcription of the transporter genes, and the newly synthesized glucose transporters are then inserted into the membrane.
optionWhy: A student who imagines insulin as a carrier for glucose picks this. Insulin is a protein that cannot cross the membrane; glucose enters through transporter proteins that the insulin signal adds to the membrane.

A student who reads 'phosphorylation of tyrosine' as the free amino acid picks this. The tyrosines phosphorylated are residues within the receptor and other proteins, and glucose enters through transporters, not bound to tyrosine.

The insulin receptor has tyrosine kinase activity: binding of the hormone outside causes phosphorylation of tyrosine inside the cell, and the resulting cascade ends with vesicles containing glucose transporters fusing with the plasma membrane, so more glucose enters.

A student who assumes more protein in the membrane requires new gene expression picks this. The transporters already exist in vesicles; the response is their movement to the plasma membrane, which is why it is fast.
questions.explain: The insulin receptor has tyrosine kinase activity: binding of the hormone outside causes phosphorylation of tyrosine inside the cell, and the resulting cascade ends with vesicles containing glucose transporters fusing with the plasma membrane, so more glucose enters.

questions.q: What is the effect of progesterone on the cells of the endometrium?
options: It causes the endometrium to break down and be shed, which is why menstruation happens while progesterone is being secreted.
It binds directly to the DNA of the endometrial cells and switches on the genes that cause growth of the lining.
It maintains and thickens the endometrium, making its glands secrete and increasing its blood supply for implantation.
It binds to receptors on the surface of endometrial cells and raises cAMP inside them, which makes the lining grow much thicker.
optionWhy: A student who attaches shedding to the hormone rather than to its withdrawal picks this. Progesterone maintains the endometrium; menstruation follows the fall in progesterone at the end of the cycle.
A student who omits the receptor picks this. Progesterone binds and activates an intracellular receptor, and it is the receptor that binds specific DNA sequences.
Progesterone acts on endometrial cells after ovulation to keep the lining thick, secretory and well supplied with blood so that an embryo can implant; a fall in progesterone leads to menstruation.
A student who places every receptor on the cell surface picks this. Progesterone is a steroid: it enters the cell and acts through an intracellular receptor that affects gene expression.
questions.explain: Progesterone acts on endometrial cells after ovulation to keep the lining thick, secretory and well supplied with blood so that an embryo can implant; a fall in progesterone leads to menstruation.

questions.q: What is the difference between negative feedback and positive feedback in the regulation of signalling pathways?
options: Negative feedback produces harmful effects in the body, whereas positive feedback produces beneficial effects.
Negative feedback lowers the level of a variable, whereas positive feedback raises the level of a variable.
Negative feedback is used in healthy regulation, whereas positive feedback occurs only when regulation has failed.
In negative feedback the response reduces the stimulus; in positive feedback the response increases it.
optionWhy: A student who carries the everyday value-judgement meaning of the words into biology picks this. The terms describe the direction of the effect on the stimulus, and both forms are normal regulation.
A student who maps negative onto 'decrease' picks this. Negative feedback opposes change in either direction, raising a variable that has fallen as readily as lowering one that has risen.
A student who has met positive feedback only as a vicious circle picks this. Positive feedback is a normal mechanism for driving processes such as ovulation and birth to completion.

Negative feedback counteracts change and keeps a variable near a set level, as when oestradiol inhibits GnRH secretion; positive feedback amplifies change and drives a process to completion, as with oxytocin during birth.
questions.explain: Negative feedback counteracts change and keeps a variable near a set level, as when oestradiol inhibits GnRH secretion; positive feedback amplifies change and drives a process to completion, as with oxytocin during birth.

questions.q: A motor neuron has its cell body in the spinal cord and a single fibre about 1 m long that reaches a muscle in the foot. What is this fibre?
options: One of the neuron's several axons, each of which reaches a different muscle in the leg.
An axon: a single long fibre along which impulses are conducted away from the cell body.
A nerve, because a fibre this long must be made of many neurons joined end to end.
A connecting fibre that links the neuron to the muscle but is not part of the neuron itself.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a neuron has several axons picks this. In fact a neuron has a single axon; its branches near the end are terminals of that one axon.
An axon is a long single fibre projecting from the cell body. A motor neuron's axon can extend about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle, and impulses are conducted along it.
A student who confuses a nerve with a neuron picks this. In fact one neuron's axon can be a metre long; a nerve is a bundle of many such fibres.
A student who sees fibres as separate wiring picks this. In fact the fibre is part of the neuron: an extension of its cytoplasm surrounded by its own membrane.
questions.explain: An axon is a long single fibre projecting from the cell body. A motor neuron's axon can extend about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle, and impulses are conducted along it.

questions.q: How does the sodium–potassium pump contribute to the resting potential of a neuron?
options: It uses energy from ATP to move potassium ions out of the neuron and sodium ions in across the membrane, building up concentration gradients of both ions.
It lets sodium and potassium ions diffuse down their concentration gradients through its channel, without using any ATP at all.
It uses energy from ATP to move sodium ions out of the neuron and potassium ions in, building up concentration gradients of both ions.
It is switched off while the neuron is at rest, so that no ATP is used until an impulse arrives at the membrane of the neuron.
optionWhy: A student who has the two ions the wrong way round picks this. In fact sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions in, so the cytoplasm is high in potassium ions and low in sodium ions.
A student who confuses a pump with a channel picks this. In fact the pump moves ions against their gradients, which requires energy from ATP; diffusion cannot build a gradient.

Energy from ATP drives the pumping of sodium and potassium ions in opposite directions across the membrane: sodium ions out and potassium ions in. The gradients this establishes, together with unequal leakage of the two ions, generate the negative resting potential.
A student who thinks 'resting' means inactive picks this. In fact the pump works continuously at rest, and it is this pumping that maintains the resting potential.
questions.explain: Energy from ATP drives the pumping of sodium and potassium ions in opposite directions across the membrane: sodium ions out and potassium ions in. The gradients this establishes, together with unequal leakage of the two ions, generate the negative resting potential.

questions.q: In a study of axon diameter and conduction speed, the correlation coefficient was r = +0.90. Which statement about the coefficient of determination is correct?
options: R² = 0.81, so about 81% of the variation in speed is explained by variation in diameter.
R² = 0.90, so about 90% of the variation in speed is explained by the variation in diameter.
R² = 0.81, so about 81% of the fibres measured conducted faster when they had a larger diameter.
R² = 0.81, which proves that a larger diameter is the cause of the faster conduction speed.
optionWhy: The coefficient of determination is the square of the correlation coefficient: 0.90² = 0.81. It evaluates the degree to which variation in the independent variable (diameter) explains the variation in the dependent variable (speed), here 81%.
A student who uses r itself as the proportion explained picks this. In fact R² is r squared, 0.81, so 81% of the variation is explained.
A student who reads R² as a fraction of data points picks this. In fact R² describes how much of the variation in speed is accounted for by diameter, not how many fibres follow the trend.
A student who treats a strong correlation as proof of cause picks this. In fact R² measures the strength of the statistical association; causation would need experimental evidence or a mechanism.
questions.explain: The coefficient of determination is the square of the correlation coefficient: 0.90² = 0.81. It evaluates the degree to which variation in the independent variable (diameter) explains the variation in the dependent variable (speed), here 81%.

questions.q: Which statement about a synapse is correct?
options: A signal can pass across it in either direction, depending on which of the two neurons is stimulated first.
It is found only where two neurons meet, so muscle fibres are stimulated directly by the nerve impulse.
A signal can pass across it in one direction only, from the presynaptic cell to the postsynaptic cell.
The action potential jumps across the gap as an electrical spark, so no chemical is needed to cross the cleft.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the synapse as a simple gap picks this. In fact only one side releases neurotransmitter and only the other has receptors, so transmission is one-way.
A student who has only seen neuron-to-neuron synapses picks this. In fact synapses also occur between neurons and effector cells; a neuromuscular junction is a synapse.
A signal can only pass in one direction across a typical synapse, because neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.
A student who assumes electricity bridges the cleft picks this. In fact the signal crosses the cleft as a neurotransmitter that diffuses to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.explain: A signal can only pass in one direction across a typical synapse, because neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.q: How does acetylcholine generate an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
options: It diffuses across the cleft and enters the postsynaptic cell, where it depolarizes the membrane from the inside.
It is actively transported across the cleft by carrier proteins, which use ATP to push it into the postsynaptic cell.
It diffuses across the cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors, opening channels through which sodium ions enter the postsynaptic cell.
It diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors, opening channels through which potassium ions enter the postsynaptic cell.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the neurotransmitter goes into the next cell picks this. In fact acetylcholine binds to receptors on the outer surface of the postsynaptic membrane and stays outside; ions entering through the opened channels cause the depolarization.

A student who thinks crossing the cleft needs active transport picks this. In fact acetylcholine diffuses across the narrow cleft and binds to receptors; it is not pumped and it does not enter the cell.

Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Binding opens channels for positively charged ions, mainly sodium ions, which enter and depolarize the membrane, producing an excitatory postsynaptic potential.

A student who has the ions swapped picks this. In fact the channels opened by acetylcholine at an excitatory synapse let sodium ions enter; potassium ions are more concentrated inside and would not enter.
questions.explain: Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to transmembrane receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Binding opens channels for positively charged ions, mainly sodium ions, which enter and depolarize the membrane, producing an excitatory postsynaptic potential.

questions.q: How do local currents propagate an action potential along an axon?
options: Sodium ions that entered at the start travel along the whole axon to its end, carrying the depolarization with them.
Sodium ions that entered diffuse to the next region and depolarize it fully, so no voltage-gated channels are needed there.
Electrons released when the sodium channels open flow along the inside of the axon, depolarizing the whole length at once.
Sodium ions that entered diffuse along the inside of the axon to the next region, bringing it to threshold so its sodium channels open.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the same ions travel the length of the axon picks this. In fact each region admits its own sodium ions once it reaches threshold; the ions that entered move only to the neighbouring region.

A student who thinks the local current carries the whole depolarization picks this. In fact local currents only bring the next region to threshold; its own voltage-gated sodium channels then produce the full depolarization.
A student who thinks the impulse is electron flow picks this. In fact local currents are movements of ions, and the action potential is regenerated region by region, not all at once.

Sodium ions entering at the depolarized region diffuse along the inside of the axon to the adjacent region, while outside the axon sodium ions diffuse towards the depolarized region. These local currents reduce the membrane potential of the adjacent region until threshold is reached and its voltage-gated sodium channels open, regenerating the action potential.
questions.explain: Sodium ions entering at the depolarized region diffuse along the inside of the axon to the adjacent region, while outside the axon sodium ions diffuse towards the depolarized region. These local currents reduce the membrane potential of the adjacent region until threshold is reached and its voltage-gated sodium channels open, regenerating the action potential.

questions.q: An oscilloscope trace of an axon shows a steady −70 mV, then a rapid rise to +30 mV at 1 ms, a fall back through −70 mV by 3 ms, a brief dip to −80 mV, and a return to −70 mV. What is happening between 1 ms and 3 ms?
options: Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels are open and potassium ions are entering the axon.
Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels are open and potassium ions are leaving the axon.
Repolarization: the sodium–potassium pump is actively moving sodium ions back out of the axon.
Depolarization: the membrane potential is becoming more negative as the polarity is being removed from it.
optionWhy: A student who has the direction of potassium movement wrong picks this. In fact potassium ions leave the axon, removing positive charge and so making the inside negative again.

The fall from the +30 mV peak back to the resting potential is repolarization. It is caused by voltage-gated potassium channels opening after the sodium channels close, so that potassium ions diffuse out and the inside becomes negative again. The dip to −80 mV is a brief hyperpolarization: the voltage-gated potassium channels are slow to close, so potassium ions continue to leave for a moment after the resting potential is reached, and the membrane returns to −70 mV once they have closed.

A student who credits the pump with repolarization picks this. In fact a fall of 100 mV in 2 ms is produced by potassium ions diffusing out through voltage-gated channels; the pump restores gradients much more slowly afterwards.
A student who thinks depolarization means becoming more negative picks this. In fact depolarization is the rise to +30 mV before 1 ms; the return to negative values is repolarization.
questions.explain: The fall from the +30 mV peak back to the resting potential is repolarization. It is caused by voltage-gated potassium channels opening after the sodium channels close, so that potassium ions diffuse out and the inside becomes negative again. The dip to −80 mV is a brief hyperpolarization: the voltage-gated potassium channels are slow to close, so potassium ions continue to leave for a moment after the resting potential is reached, and the membrane returns to −70 mV once they have closed.

questions.q: How do neonicotinoid pesticides block synaptic transmission in insects?
options: They block the reuptake of acetylcholine into the presynaptic neuron, so the insect's synapses soon run out of neurotransmitter.
They inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, so acetylcholine is not broken down at all after it has been released.
They prevent calcium ions from crossing the synaptic cleft, so the postsynaptic membrane is not depolarized at all.
They bind to acetylcholine receptors at the insect's synapses, so acetylcholine can no longer transmit signals across them.
optionWhy: A student who has merged the two examples picks this. In fact blocking reuptake is the mechanism of cocaine; neonicotinoids act at the acetylcholine receptors.
A student who expects a pesticide to target the enzyme picks this. In fact that is the action of other insecticides; neonicotinoids bind to the receptors, not the enzyme.
A student who thinks calcium crosses the cleft picks this. In fact calcium acts inside the presynaptic neuron, and neonicotinoids act on the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.

Neonicotinoids bind to acetylcholine receptors on postsynaptic membranes in the insect's central nervous system. The receptors can then no longer respond normally to acetylcholine, so synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed and dies.
questions.explain: Neonicotinoids bind to acetylcholine receptors on postsynaptic membranes in the insect's central nervous system. The receptors can then no longer respond normally to acetylcholine, so synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed and dies.

questions.q: What happens at the postsynaptic membrane when an inhibitory neurotransmitter binds to its receptors?
options: Channels open that make the inside more negative than the resting potential, so the membrane is hyperpolarized and further from threshold.
Channels open that depolarize the membrane, but by a smaller amount than an excitatory neurotransmitter would.
Channels open that make the inside more positive than the resting potential, which is called hyperpolarization.
Nothing happens at this membrane, because inhibitory neurotransmitters act by stopping release from the presynaptic neuron.
optionWhy: Inhibitory neurotransmitters open channels that let negative ions such as chloride ions in or positive ions such as potassium ions out. The postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarized, generating an inhibitory postsynaptic potential that makes an action potential less likely.
A student who thinks 'inhibitory' just means 'weaker' picks this. In fact inhibitory neurotransmitters move the membrane potential the opposite way, making it more negative.
A student who reads 'hyper' as 'more positive' picks this. In fact hyperpolarization means more polarized: more negative inside than at rest.
A student who thinks inhibition switches off the presynaptic neuron picks this. In fact the inhibitory neurotransmitter is itself released and acts on the postsynaptic membrane, hyperpolarizing it.
questions.explain: Inhibitory neurotransmitters open channels that let negative ions such as chloride ions in or positive ions such as potassium ions out. The postsynaptic membrane becomes hyperpolarized, generating an inhibitory postsynaptic potential that makes an action potential less likely.

questions.q: Eating chilli peppers causes a burning pain in the mouth. Which explanation is correct?
options: Capsaicin raises the temperature of the tissue in the mouth, and this heat is what the free nerve endings then detect.
Capsaicin stimulates free nerve endings, which perceive the pain in the mouth and then send a report of it to the brain.
Capsaicin causes receptor cells in the mouth to release neurotransmitter onto sensory neurons, which then carry the pain.
Capsaicin opens channels for positive ions in free nerve endings, so threshold is reached and impulses pass to the brain, where pain is perceived.
optionWhy: A student who takes 'hot' literally picks this. In fact the tissue does not warm; capsaicin opens the same channels that heat opens, so the brain perceives the same burning.
A student who locates perception at the site of the stimulus picks this. In fact the nerve endings only detect the stimulus and generate impulses; pain is perceived in the brain.
A student who expects separate receptor cells picks this. In fact the free nerve endings are part of the sensory neurons themselves, and capsaicin acts directly on their ion channels.

Free nerve endings have channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or chemicals such as capsaicin. Entry of positive ions brings the membrane to threshold, and the impulses that result pass to the brain, where the pain is perceived.
questions.explain: Free nerve endings have channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or chemicals such as capsaicin. Entry of positive ions brings the membrane to threshold, and the impulses that result pass to the brain, where the pain is perceived.
